bringing a crop variety from one region or country into a new area where it was not previously grown
crossing two plants of the same variety
removing undesirable plants from a field
questions.explanation: Introduction involves transferring seeds or planting material of a crop variety from its place of origin to a new locality for cultivation and evaluation.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Plant breeding, broadly, is the science and practice of
options: harvesting mature crops from the field
storing seeds for the next planting season
controlling weeds in a cropped field
developing new or improved crop varieties with desirable traits
questions.explanation: Plant breeding combines methods such as selection, hybridisation, and introduction to systematically develop crop varieties with improved agronomic characteristics.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: A high-yielding crop variety is one that
options: matures much later than local varieties
is highly susceptible to common pests
produces significantly more output per unit area than the local/unimproved variety
requires no water or sunlight to grow
questions.explanation: High-yielding varieties are specifically bred or selected to give greater output (grain, tuber, or fruit) per unit area compared to traditional local varieties.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Disease resistance, as an aim of crop improvement, means the improved variety can
options: be planted only once in a lifetime
grow without any soil nutrients
withstand or resist infection by specific pathogens better than susceptible varieties
germinate without light or water
questions.explanation: Disease-resistant varieties possess genetic traits that reduce the severity of infection or damage caused by particular pathogens, lowering crop losses.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Which of the following is an example of using introduction as a crop improvement method in West Africa?
options: Selecting the best local plants from an existing farm
Crossing two local varieties of cassava on the same farm
Bringing improved maize varieties bred in another country into local cultivation
Applying fertiliser to an existing crop
questions.explanation: Introduction specifically involves transferring planting material developed elsewhere into a new farming area, as is often done with improved maize or rice varieties.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Weeds can be classified based on their life cycle into
options: only edible and inedible weeds
annual, biennial, and perennial weeds
only red and green weeds
only tall and short weeds
questions.explanation: Like crops, weeds are classified by life cycle length: annuals complete their cycle in one season, biennials in two, and perennials live for many years.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Based on their botanical characteristics, weeds are commonly classified into
options: root crops and fibre crops only
cereals and legumes only
beverage crops and spice crops only
grasses, sedges, and broad-leaved weeds
questions.explanation: Weeds are broadly grouped botanically into narrow-leaved grasses, sedges (with triangular stems), and broad-leaved weeds, which differ in structure and control methods.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: The economic importance of weeds in crop production is mainly that they
options: always increase crop yield significantly
reduce crop yield through competition, though some also have medicinal or fodder value
eliminate the need for soil nutrients
never affect the growth of cultivated crops
questions.explanation: While weeds are primarily harmful due to competition with crops, some weed species have redeeming value as livestock fodder, medicinal plants, or soil cover.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Weeds are commonly dispersed from one location to another mainly by
options: soil pH changes only
photosynthesis alone
crop rotation practices only
wind, water, animals, and farm implements
questions.explanation: Weed seeds and vegetative parts are spread by natural agents like wind and water, by animals (in dung or fur), and unintentionally by farm tools and machinery.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Cultural control of weeds includes practices such as
options: introducing insect predators of weeds
using a hoe to physically uproot weeds
crop rotation, proper spacing, and timely planting to suppress weed growth
spraying chemical herbicides only
questions.explanation: Cultural weed control relies on farming practices, such as rotation, close spacing, and mulching, that make conditions less favourable for weed establishment.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Biological control of weeds involves the use of
options: living organisms such as insects or pathogens that specifically attack the weed
mechanical ploughing
chemical herbicides
manual hand-pulling
questions.explanation: Biological weed control introduces natural enemies, such as specific insects or plant pathogens, that target and suppress a particular weed species.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Chemical control of weeds is achieved through the application of
options: fungicides
acaricides
insecticides
herbicides
questions.explanation: Herbicides are chemicals specifically formulated to kill or inhibit the growth of unwanted weeds without excessively damaging the crop.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Mechanical control of weeds includes methods such as
options: spraying with 2,4-D herbicide
crop rotation with legumes
hoeing, ploughing, and manual hand-pulling
introducing a weed-eating insect
questions.explanation: Mechanical control physically removes or destroys weeds using tools or machinery, such as hoeing, ploughing, or hand-weeding.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: A selective herbicide is one that
options: kills specific target weeds without seriously harming the crop
kills all plants it comes into contact with
has no effect on any plant species
controls insect pests rather than weeds
questions.explanation: Selective herbicides are formulated to be toxic to certain weed species (e.g., broad-leaved weeds in a cereal crop) while leaving the crop largely unharmed.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: A non-selective (total) herbicide is one that
options: affects only grasses and not broad-leaved plants
controls only sedges
affects only underground weed roots
kills or damages virtually all plants it is applied to, regardless of species
questions.explanation: Non-selective herbicides, such as glyphosate, act on almost all green plants they contact, so they must be used carefully to avoid harming the crop.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Imperata cylindrica (spear grass), a troublesome perennial weed in the tropics, is difficult to control mainly because it
options: is limited to only very wet soils
reproduces only by wind-blown seed
cannot survive burning or cutting
spreads rapidly through underground rhizomes
questions.explanation: Spear grass propagates aggressively through extensive underground rhizomes, allowing it to regenerate quickly even after cutting or burning, making it hard to eradicate.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Grasshoppers and caterpillars damage crops mainly through
options: piercing and sucking plant sap
transmitting only viral diseases
boring tunnels inside stems only
biting and chewing plant leaves and tissues
questions.explanation: Grasshoppers and caterpillars have chewing mouthparts adapted for biting off and consuming leaf tissue, causing visible defoliation damage.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Aphids and cotton stainers are classified as pests that damage crops by
options: chewing large holes in leaves
piercing plant tissue and sucking sap
boring into stems and tunnelling
attacking only stored grain
questions.explanation: Aphids and cotton stainers have specialised piercing-sucking mouthparts used to penetrate plant tissue and extract sap, weakening the plant and sometimes spreading disease.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Weevils and stem borers are classified as pests that damage crops mainly by
options: attacking only the root hairs of seedlings
boring into and tunnelling through plant stems, grains, or tubers
feeding exclusively on flower nectar
sucking sap from the underside of leaves
questions.explanation: Weevils and stem borers bore into and tunnel through plant tissues such as stems, stored grains, or tubers, causing internal damage often not visible until severe.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Which of the following is a major biting and chewing insect pest of crops?
options: Weevil
Grasshopper
Aphid
Cotton stainer
questions.explanation: The grasshopper uses strong mandibles to bite and chew plant leaves, classifying it among biting/chewing pests, unlike sap-sucking aphids or boring weevils.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Maize rust, a common fungal disease of maize, is easily recognised by the appearance of
options: sudden wilting with no visible leaf symptoms
white powdery patches on the roots only
reddish-brown pustules on the leaves
black soot covering the whole plant
questions.explanation: Maize rust is characterised by small, reddish-brown, powdery pustules that develop on the leaf surface, caused by rust fungi such as Puccinia species.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Cassava mosaic disease, a major viral disease of cassava, is characterised mainly by
options: white cottony growth on the roots
reddish-brown pustules on the stem
a mottled pattern of light and dark green patches on the leaves
complete blackening and rotting of the tuber
questions.explanation: Cassava mosaic virus produces a characteristic mosaic pattern of yellow-green and dark green patches on the leaves, often accompanied by leaf distortion and stunted growth.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Cassava mosaic disease is mainly spread from plant to plant by
options: soil-borne bacteria
whiteflies and the use of infected stem cuttings
wind-blown spores alone
grasshoppers chewing on leaves
questions.explanation: The disease is transmitted by whitefly vectors feeding on infected plants and also spreads when farmers unknowingly propagate cassava using cuttings from infected plants.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Yam anthracnose, a destructive fungal disease of yam, is characterised by
options: powdery white mildew covering the whole plant
swelling and distortion of the tuber only
a mosaic pattern of yellow and green on leaves
dark, sunken lesions on leaves and stems, often with concentric rings
questions.explanation: Yam anthracnose produces dark, sunken spots on leaves and stems that often show concentric ring patterns, and can severely defoliate the vine if untreated.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Cocoa black pod disease, caused by a fungus-like pathogen (Phytophthora), is characterised mainly by
options: white powdery growth on the trunk only
swelling of the roots
dark brown to black lesions that spread over and eventually rot the pod
yellowing of the leaves only, with no effect on pods
questions.explanation: Black pod disease causes brown-to-black lesions on cocoa pods that rapidly enlarge, rotting the pod and destroying the beans inside, causing major yield losses.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Groundnut rosette disease, a major viral disease of groundnut, is characterised by
options: a strong, pleasant fragrance from infected leaves
increased pod and seed size
large sunken lesions on the pod shell only
stunted, bushy growth with mottled or chlorotic leaves
questions.explanation: Groundnut rosette virus causes severe stunting, a bushy 'rosette' appearance, and mottled yellow-green (chlorotic) leaves, drastically reducing yield.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Groundnut rosette disease is mainly transmitted from plant to plant by
options: aphids
stem borers
nematodes
whiteflies
questions.explanation: Groundnut rosette virus is transmitted by aphid vectors feeding on infected plants and moving to healthy ones, spreading the disease rapidly within a field.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: The causal organism of maize rust belongs to which broad group of pathogens?
options: Fungi
Viruses
Nematodes
Bacteria
questions.explanation: Maize rust is caused by rust fungi (e.g., Puccinia species), which produce characteristic spore-filled pustules on infected leaves.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: The causal organism of cassava mosaic disease belongs to which broad group of pathogens?
options: Bacterium
Fungus
Virus
Nematode
questions.explanation: Cassava mosaic disease is caused by cassava mosaic viruses, transmitted mainly by whiteflies and through infected planting material.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Management of crop diseases such as cassava mosaic and groundnut rosette relies heavily on
options: reducing soil fertility deliberately
increasing the plant population density only
planting only during the dry season regardless of the crop
using disease-free planting material and resistant varieties, and controlling insect vectors
questions.explanation: Since these diseases spread via infected cuttings/seed and insect vectors, control focuses on clean planting material, resistant varieties, and vector (whitefly/aphid) control.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Fungal crop diseases such as maize rust, yam anthracnose, and cocoa black pod are commonly controlled by
options: application of herbicides
use of insecticides only
irrigation alone
timely application of appropriate fungicides
questions.explanation: Fungicides are chemical agents specifically formulated to prevent or control fungal infections such as rusts, anthracnose, and pod rots.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Which of the following is a symptom commonly associated with piercing and sucking insect pest damage on crops?
options: Tunnels bored through the stem
Large, ragged holes chewed out of leaves
Complete uprooting of the plant
Yellowing, curling, or wilting of leaves due to sap loss
questions.explanation: Piercing-sucking pests like aphids withdraw plant sap, often causing leaves to yellow, curl, or wilt, distinct from the ragged chewing damage of biting pests.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: The cotton stainer is an important pest mainly of which crop?
options: Cocoa
Cotton
Rice
Yam
questions.explanation: The cotton stainer feeds on cotton bolls, piercing and sucking the seeds, which stains the lint and reduces both quality and yield of the cotton crop.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Stem borers cause damage to cereal crops mainly by
options: living exclusively in stored grain
attacking only the flowers
sucking sap from the root hairs
tunnelling into the stem, weakening it and disrupting nutrient/water transport
questions.explanation: Stem borer larvae tunnel inside the stem of cereals like maize, damaging vascular tissue, weakening the plant, and often causing 'dead heart' or lodging.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Farm animals with a simple, single-chambered stomach, such as pigs and poultry, are classified as
options: monogastric animals
ruminants
polygastric animals only
amphibians
questions.explanation: Monogastric animals possess a single-compartment stomach and rely mainly on enzymatic digestion, unlike ruminants, which have a multi-chambered stomach.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Ruminant animals, such as cattle, goats, and sheep, possess a stomach with how many compartments?
options: Four
Two
Three
One
questions.explanation: The ruminant stomach comprises four compartments: the rumen, reticulum, omasum, and abomasum, which together enable efficient digestion of fibrous plant material.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: In the ruminant digestive system, the compartment mainly responsible for microbial fermentation of fibrous feed is the
options: omasum
reticulum
rumen
abomasum
questions.explanation: The rumen is the largest stomach compartment, housing billions of microorganisms that ferment cellulose and other fibrous material before further digestion.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: The abomasum in a ruminant's stomach is often referred to as the
options: rumen
omasum
reticulum
true (glandular) stomach
questions.explanation: The abomasum secretes digestive enzymes and acid similar to a monogastric stomach, earning it the name 'true stomach' among the four ruminant compartments.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Cud, which ruminant animals regurgitate and re-chew, is partially digested food returned from the
options: rumen and reticulum
small intestine
large intestine
abomasum
questions.explanation: Ruminants regurgitate coarsely fermented material from the rumen/reticulum back to the mouth for further chewing (rumination), improving digestion of fibrous feed.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: The female reproductive organ responsible for producing eggs (ova) in mammals is the
options: ovary
oviduct
vagina
uterus
questions.explanation: The ovaries are the primary female reproductive organs responsible for producing ova (eggs) and secreting reproductive hormones.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: The estrus (oestrous) cycle in female mammals refers to the
options: single event of giving birth
recurring physiological cycle of reproductive readiness, culminating in ovulation
process of milk production
growth phase before puberty
questions.explanation: The estrus cycle is the repeating series of hormonal and physical changes that prepare a female mammal for mating and ovulation until pregnancy occurs.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Gestation period refers to the
options: duration of pregnancy from conception to birth
period from birth to weaning
time taken for an egg to hatch
interval between two successive heat periods
questions.explanation: Gestation is the length of pregnancy, varying by species: about 283 days in cattle, 150 days in sheep/goats, and 114 days in pigs.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Parturition refers to the
options: period of heat in a female animal
act of giving birth to young
onset of puberty in an animal
process of milk let-down
questions.explanation: Parturition is the biological process of delivering offspring at the end of gestation.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Lactation refers to the
options: process of giving birth
production and secretion of milk by the mammary glands
period of feed withdrawal before slaughter
onset of the estrus cycle
questions.explanation: Lactation is the physiological process by which the mammary glands synthesise and secrete milk to nourish the newborn.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Which of the following animals is classified as a monogastric (non-ruminant) animal?
options: Goat
Pig
Sheep
Cattle
questions.explanation: Pigs have a simple, single-chambered stomach and are classified as monogastric animals, unlike cattle, goats, and sheep, which are ruminants.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: The intensive system of livestock management is characterised mainly by
options: raising only wild animals with no human management
allowing animals to roam freely over a wide area with no housing
confining animals in a limited space with all feed and water supplied by the farmer
a combination of free-range grazing and occasional supplementary feeding
questions.explanation: Intensive management confines animals (e.g., in cages, pens, or feedlots) with all their feed, water, and care fully controlled by the farmer, maximising output per unit area.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: The extensive system of livestock management is characterised mainly by
options: raising animals exclusively indoors under controlled lighting
animals being allowed to roam and graze freely over a large area with minimal supervision
total confinement with artificial feeding only
animals being kept permanently in cages
questions.explanation: Extensive systems, common with cattle in open rangeland, allow animals to graze over large areas naturally, with limited direct management or supplementary feeding.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: The semi-intensive system of livestock management combines features of both intensive and extensive systems by
options: keeping animals fully confined at all times with no access to pasture
allowing animals to roam entirely freely with no supplementary feed at all
raising animals only in water bodies
allowing animals some access to open range/pasture while also providing supplementary housing and feed
questions.explanation: Semi-intensive management gives animals partial access to pasture or a range area while still supplying housing, supplementary feed, and closer supervision than pure extensive systems.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: In poultry management, day-old chicks are provided with supplementary heat through a process called
options: culling
weaning
debeaking
brooding
questions.explanation: Brooding supplies artificial warmth to chicks that cannot yet regulate their own body temperature, essential during the first few weeks of life.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Debeaking in poultry management is carried out mainly to
options: improve the flavour of poultry meat
prevent respiratory diseases
increase the rate of egg-laying directly
reduce injurious pecking and cannibalism among birds in confinement
questions.explanation: Trimming part of the beak reduces the damage from pecking and cannibalistic behaviour, which is more common when birds are kept closely confined.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Culling in livestock and poultry management refers to the
options: removal of unproductive, sick, or otherwise undesirable animals from the flock/herd
act of selecting the best breeding stock only
process of vaccinating animals against disease
process of weaning young animals
questions.explanation: Culling systematically removes animals that are unproductive, diseased, or of poor quality, improving the overall performance and health of the remaining flock or herd.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: In cattle management, the process of removing the horn buds from young calves is called
options: dehorning
branding
castration
docking
questions.explanation: Dehorning removes horns or horn buds to reduce injury to handlers and other animals, and is usually performed while the animal is young.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Castration in livestock management refers to the
options: act of tagging an animal's ear for identification
removal or destruction of the testes in a male animal
process of weaning a young animal
process of removing the horns
questions.explanation: Castration removes or disables the testes of male animals not intended for breeding, making them calmer and improving meat quality for fattening.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Weaning in livestock management refers to the
options: act of branding an animal for identification
gradual withdrawal of young animals from dependence on their mother's milk to solid feed
process of assisting an animal during birth
removal of a female animal's ovaries
questions.explanation: Weaning is the transition process where young animals stop suckling and begin to rely on solid feed for nutrition.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Ear tagging and branding of livestock are practices carried out mainly for
options: identification and record-keeping of individual animals
controlling internal parasites
curing bacterial infections
increasing the animal's growth rate directly
questions.explanation: Ear tags and brand marks give each animal a unique identifier, enabling farmers to track breeding, health treatments, and production records accurately.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: From hatching to the point of lay, a young female chicken raised for egg production is generally referred to as a
options: cockerel
capon
hen
pullet
questions.explanation: A pullet is a young female chicken that has not yet started laying eggs; once she begins laying, she is referred to as a hen.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Proper livestock housing is important mainly because it
options: protects animals from harsh weather, predators, and aids disease control
eliminates the need for feeding animals
guarantees a fixed market price for produce
replaces the need for a balanced diet
questions.explanation: Good housing shelters livestock from extreme weather and predators, while also making feeding, sanitation, and disease control much easier to manage.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Proteins in livestock nutrition are important mainly for
options: insulating the body against cold
growth and repair of body tissues
providing the primary source of energy under normal conditions
lubricating the joints
questions.explanation: Dietary protein supplies amino acids essential for building and repairing muscles and other body tissues, especially important for young, growing animals.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Carbohydrates in livestock feed serve mainly as a source of
options: essential minerals for bone formation
vitamins needed for metabolism
building blocks for muscle tissue
energy for body maintenance and productive functions
questions.explanation: Carbohydrates are the main, readily available energy source in most livestock rations, fuelling maintenance, growth, and production activities.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Fats and oils in livestock nutrition provide
options: no useful nutritional value to the animal
the primary material for building muscle tissue
only minerals required for bone growth
a concentrated source of energy, more than twice that of carbohydrates per unit weight
questions.explanation: Fats and oils supply about twice the energy of an equal weight of carbohydrates or protein, making them a concentrated energy source in animal diets.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Minerals such as calcium and phosphorus are especially important in livestock nutrition for
options: providing the main source of dietary energy
building muscle tissue exclusively
regulating body temperature directly
proper bone and teeth formation
questions.explanation: Calcium and phosphorus are key structural minerals required for strong bone and teeth development, and their deficiency can cause rickets or weak bones.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Vitamins are required in livestock diets mainly in
options: very large quantities, as a main energy source
small quantities, to regulate various metabolic processes
amounts greater than water requirements
amounts equal to protein requirements
questions.explanation: Vitamins are needed only in small amounts but play essential roles in regulating metabolism, vision, reproduction, and immune function.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Water is considered an essential nutrient in livestock nutrition mainly because it
options: is only needed by animals kept in hot climates
is required for nearly all metabolic processes and regulates body temperature
provides the highest amount of energy of all nutrients
is the main source of protein for growth
questions.explanation: Water is vital for digestion, nutrient transport, waste removal, and thermoregulation, and its lack quickly causes more severe effects than deficiency of any other nutrient.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Roughages, as a feed category for livestock, are characterised mainly by
options: high fibre content and relatively low energy concentration
containing no nutritional value at all
very high energy and very low fibre content
being composed entirely of animal protein
questions.explanation: Roughages, such as hay, grass, and silage, contain high levels of fibre (cellulose) and are lower in energy concentration compared to concentrate feeds.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Concentrates, as a feed category for livestock, are characterised mainly by
options: being suitable only for ruminant animals
low fibre content and high energy and/or protein concentration
having no digestible nutrients at all
very high fibre content and low energy
questions.explanation: Concentrate feeds, such as grains and oil-seed cakes, are low in fibre but dense in energy and/or protein, used to supplement roughage-based diets.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: A deficiency of protein in the diet of young growing animals commonly results in
options: stunted growth and poor development
improved disease resistance
increased bone strength
excessive fat deposition only
questions.explanation: Insufficient dietary protein deprives growing animals of the amino acids needed for tissue development, leading to stunted growth and poor body condition.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: A deficiency of calcium in laying hens commonly results in
options: thin-shelled or soft-shelled eggs
excessively thick eggshells
an increase in egg size
improved feather quality
questions.explanation: Calcium is a major component of eggshell; inadequate dietary calcium in laying hens leads to thin, weak, or soft-shelled eggs and reduced shell quality.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Feed formulation for livestock involves
options: randomly mixing any available feed materials
combining different feed ingredients in the correct proportions to meet an animal's nutrient requirements
feeding an animal only one type of feed ingredient at all times
withholding all feed for a set period before slaughter only
questions.explanation: Feed formulation is the deliberate, calculated combination of feed ingredients to supply the correct balance of energy, protein, minerals, and vitamins for a particular class of livestock.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Malnutrition in livestock refers to a condition resulting from
options: an improper balance or insufficient supply of essential nutrients in the diet
excessive supply of clean drinking water
overuse of vaccination programmes
too much exercise and free-range movement
questions.explanation: Malnutrition arises when an animal's diet lacks the correct balance or amount of essential nutrients, leading to poor growth, weakness, or disease susceptibility.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Rinderpest is a highly contagious disease of cattle caused by a
options: fungus
virus
bacterium
protozoan
questions.explanation: Rinderpest, historically one of the most devastating cattle diseases, is caused by a morbillivirus, though it has since been declared globally eradicated.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Foot-and-mouth disease, which primarily affects cloven-hoofed animals, is caused by a
options: protozoan parasite
virus
fungus
bacterium
questions.explanation: Foot-and-mouth disease is caused by a highly contagious virus that produces blisters on the mouth, feet, and teats of cloven-hoofed livestock.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Newcastle disease, a devastating viral disease of poultry, is characterised by symptoms such as
options: respiratory distress, greenish diarrhoea, and nervous signs (twisted neck)
excessive weight gain and improved egg production
swelling of the leg joints only, with no other symptoms
improved feather growth and appetite
questions.explanation: Newcastle disease produces respiratory signs, greenish diarrhoea, and characteristic nervous symptoms such as twisted neck (torticollis) and paralysis in severe cases.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Gumboro disease (infectious bursal disease) mainly affects the
options: bursa of Fabricius, weakening the immune system of young poultry
gills of pond fish
hooves of cattle and goats
udder of dairy cows
questions.explanation: Gumboro disease damages the bursa of Fabricius, a key immune organ in young chickens, leaving affected birds highly susceptible to other infections.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Anthrax, a serious disease affecting livestock and potentially humans, is caused by a
options: roundworm
bacterium
protozoan
virus
questions.explanation: Anthrax is caused by the spore-forming bacterium Bacillus anthracis, which can infect livestock and is transmissible to humans (a zoonotic disease).

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Brucellosis, a bacterial disease of cattle that can also infect humans, mainly causes
options: improved milk yield in infected cows
abortion and infertility in affected animals
immediate death within hours of infection in all cases
no effect on reproduction at all
questions.explanation: Brucellosis is well known for causing abortion, retained placenta, and reduced fertility in cattle, and is also a zoonotic risk to farm workers.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Tuberculosis in cattle, caused by a bacterium, is of particular public health concern because it
options: cannot spread between animals or to humans at all
improves the animal's growth rate
can be transmitted to humans, especially through unpasteurised milk
only affects the animal's skin, with no internal effects
questions.explanation: Bovine tuberculosis is a zoonotic bacterial disease that can be transmitted to humans, particularly through consumption of unpasteurised milk from infected cattle.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Fowl cholera, a bacterial disease of poultry, commonly causes
options: immunity to all other poultry diseases
improved appetite and weight gain
increased egg production
sudden death, fever, and greenish-yellow diarrhoea in affected birds
questions.explanation: Fowl cholera, caused by Pasteurella multocida, often causes sudden death in acute cases, along with fever, ruffled feathers, and greenish-yellow diarrhoea.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Trypanosomiasis, a disease of major economic importance to livestock in Africa, is caused by a
options: bacterium transmitted through contaminated water
protozoan parasite transmitted by the tsetse fly
virus transmitted by mosquitoes
fungus found in damp bedding
questions.explanation: Trypanosomiasis (nagana in cattle) is caused by Trypanosoma protozoa, transmitted mainly by the bite of the tsetse fly, and severely limits cattle rearing in tsetse-infested areas.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Coccidiosis, a common disease of young poultry, is caused by
options: roundworms found in the liver
a bacterium spread through the air
protozoan parasites that damage the intestinal lining
a virus that attacks the respiratory system
questions.explanation: Coccidiosis is caused by Eimeria protozoan parasites that invade and damage the intestinal lining, causing bloody diarrhoea, especially in young chicks.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Tapeworms and roundworms affecting livestock are classified as
options: vectors only, not parasites
endoparasites
beneficial gut microorganisms
ectoparasites
questions.explanation: Tapeworms and roundworms live inside the host's body (e.g., in the intestines), classifying them as endoparasites, as opposed to external ectoparasites.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Liver flukes are internal parasites of livestock that mainly reside and cause damage in the
options: skin surface
outer ear only
feathers of poultry
liver and bile ducts
questions.explanation: Liver flukes are flatworms that migrate to and inhabit the liver and bile ducts of infected animals, causing liver damage and reduced productivity.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Ticks, lice, and mites affecting livestock are classified as
options: vectors that cause no direct harm
beneficial symbiotic organisms
endoparasites
ectoparasites
questions.explanation: Ticks, lice, and mites live and feed on the external body surface of the host animal, classifying them as ectoparasites, unlike internal endoparasites.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Tsetse flies are of major economic importance to livestock production mainly because they
options: act only as pollinators of pasture grasses
improve the fertility of infected animals
transmit trypanosomiasis (nagana) among cattle
feed only on plant sap and cause no harm to animals
questions.explanation: Tsetse flies are the primary vectors of Trypanosoma parasites, transmitting trypanosomiasis (nagana), a disease that severely limits cattle rearing across large parts of Africa.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Endoparasites differ from ectoparasites mainly in that endoparasites
options: live inside the host's body, while ectoparasites live on its external surface
are always transmitted only by biting insects
cannot cause any disease in the host
are always larger in size than ectoparasites
questions.explanation: The key distinction is location: endoparasites (e.g., tapeworms, liver flukes) live internally, whereas ectoparasites (e.g., ticks, lice) attach to and live on the external body surface.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Vaccination of livestock and poultry is carried out mainly to
options: eliminate all external and internal parasites at once
stimulate the animal's immune system to resist specific infectious diseases
provide the animal with all its essential nutrients
increase the animal's body weight directly
questions.explanation: Vaccines expose the immune system to a weakened or inactivated form of a pathogen, prompting the development of protective immunity against future natural infection.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Which control measure is most effective specifically against ectoparasites such as ticks and mites?
options: Regular dipping or spraying with acaricides
Deworming with an anthelmintic drug
Provision of a high-protein diet
Vaccination against viral disease
questions.explanation: Acaricides applied through dipping or spraying kill external parasites like ticks and mites, while anthelmintics are used specifically against internal worm infections.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Deworming of livestock, using anthelmintic drugs, is carried out mainly to control
options: external parasites such as ticks and lice
viral diseases such as Newcastle disease
internal parasites such as roundworms and tapeworms
bacterial diseases such as anthrax
questions.explanation: Anthelmintic drugs are specifically formulated to kill or expel internal worm parasites (endoparasites) such as roundworms, tapeworms, and liver flukes from the host's body.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Aquaculture refers to the
options: study of ocean tides and currents
deliberate rearing and management of fish and other aquatic organisms under controlled conditions
capture of wild fish from the open sea
processing of fish into canned products only
questions.explanation: Aquaculture, unlike wild capture fisheries, involves the controlled breeding, feeding, and harvesting of fish and other aquatic organisms in ponds, tanks, or cages.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Establishing a fish pond requires careful consideration of factors such as
options: the price of fish in distant urban markets only
the political boundaries of the local government area
water source and supply, soil type (for water retention), and topography of the site
the number of nearby schools
questions.explanation: A good fish pond site needs a reliable water source, soil that holds water well (e.g., clayey soil), and a gentle slope to allow filling and draining.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Stocking density in a fish pond refers to the
options: amount of feed given to fish daily
number of fish stocked per unit area or volume of water
type of fish species chosen for farming
depth of water in the pond
questions.explanation: Stocking density describes how many fish are introduced per unit area/volume of pond water; overstocking can lead to poor growth and disease due to overcrowding.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Feeding of pond fish in aquaculture is typically done using
options: formulated fish feed and/or supplementary natural feed
untreated industrial waste
herbicides mixed into the pond water
only chemical fertiliser applied directly to fish
questions.explanation: Farmed fish are commonly fed nutritionally balanced formulated feeds, sometimes supplemented by natural food organisms encouraged to grow in the pond.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Harvesting of pond fish is commonly carried out by
options: waiting for fish to jump out of the pond on their own
applying pesticide to force fish to the surface
draining the pond partially or fully and netting the fish
digging up the pond bed with a plough
questions.explanation: Fish are commonly harvested by partially or completely draining the pond and using nets to collect them, or by seine netting without full drainage.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Good water quality in a fish pond is important mainly because it affects the
options: cost of pond construction only
type of fencing material used around the pond
level of dissolved oxygen and overall health/growth of the fish
colour of the pond embankment
questions.explanation: Water quality parameters such as dissolved oxygen, temperature, and pollution levels directly affect fish respiration, growth, and susceptibility to disease.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Apiculture refers to the
options: cultivation of beverage crops such as cocoa
keeping and management of bees, mainly for honey and wax production
rearing of poultry for egg production
farming of fish in ponds
questions.explanation: Apiculture (bee-keeping) involves managing colonies of honeybees in hives to produce honey, beeswax, and other products, and to aid crop pollination.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: A bee hive used in apiculture serves mainly to
options: trap and kill unwanted insect pests
store harvested crop produce
provide a controlled, artificial home for a bee colony to live and produce honey
provide drinking water for livestock
questions.explanation: A hive gives bees a structured, manageable habitat in which to build comb, raise brood, and store honey, making harvesting and management easier for the bee-keeper.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Honey harvested from bee hives is valued mainly for its use as a
options: raw material for making cotton textiles
primary source of animal feed protein
chemical pesticide against crop pests
natural sweetener and traditional medicine
questions.explanation: Honey is prized as a natural sweetening agent and has traditional uses in folk medicine, in addition to being a marketable farm product.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Bees are economically important to crop farmers, beyond honey production, mainly because they
options: prevent soil erosion around farmland
consume large amounts of crop pests directly
fix atmospheric nitrogen in the soil
pollinate flowers, improving fruit and seed set in many crops
questions.explanation: As they forage for nectar, bees transfer pollen between flowers, improving pollination and increasing fruit and seed yield in many insect-pollinated crops.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: The law of demand states that, all other factors being equal, as the price of a commodity rises, the
options: quantity supplied of it falls
quantity demanded of it falls
price of substitute goods falls
quantity demanded of it also rises
questions.explanation: The law of demand describes an inverse relationship between price and quantity demanded: as price increases, consumers generally buy less, all else being equal.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: The law of supply states that, all other factors being equal, as the price of a commodity rises, the
options: quantity supplied of it also rises
quantity demanded of it rises
quantity supplied of it falls
cost of production automatically falls
questions.explanation: The law of supply describes a direct relationship between price and quantity supplied: producers are generally willing to supply more of a good as its price rises.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Price elasticity of demand measures the
options: amount of a commodity supplied at a fixed price
total revenue earned from selling a commodity
cost of producing an extra unit of output
responsiveness of quantity demanded to a change in price
questions.explanation: Price elasticity of demand quantifies how much the quantity demanded of a good changes in response to a change in its price.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Highly perishable agricultural produce, such as tomatoes, typically has demand and/or supply that is
options: completely unaffected by price changes
relatively inelastic in the short run, since produce must be sold quickly before spoilage
perfectly elastic at all times
always in permanent short supply regardless of season
questions.explanation: Because perishables cannot easily be stored, farmers are often forced to sell quickly regardless of price, making short-run supply relatively inelastic (unresponsive to price changes).

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Non-perishable agricultural produce, such as grains that can be stored for a long period, generally allows farmers to
options: hold back produce and sell when prices are more favourable
ignore market demand completely
avoid storage costs entirely
always sell immediately regardless of market price
questions.explanation: Storable, non-perishable produce gives farmers flexibility to delay sales until prices improve, unlike perishables, which must be sold quickly.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Land, as a factor of production in agriculture, is unique mainly because its total physical supply is
options: irrelevant to agricultural output
unlimited and can always be expanded
fixed and cannot be increased
identical in fertility everywhere
questions.explanation: Unlike labour or capital, the total quantity of land available is essentially fixed, although its usable productivity can be enhanced through improved management.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Labour, as a factor of agricultural production, refers to
options: the natural resources used in production
the human physical and mental effort applied in farming activities
the organisational and risk-bearing role of the farm manager
the money and equipment invested in the farm
questions.explanation: Labour represents the human effort, whether manual or skilled, applied to carry out farming operations such as planting, weeding, and harvesting.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Capital, as a factor of agricultural production, refers to
options: man-made resources such as money, tools, machinery, and buildings used in farming
the risk-taking and organisational skill of the farmer
the physical effort of farm workers
the natural fertility of farmland
questions.explanation: Capital comprises man-made inputs, funds, equipment, and infrastructure, used alongside land and labour to carry out agricultural production.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Management (entrepreneurship), as a factor of agricultural production, refers mainly to the
options: organisation of other factors of production and the bearing of business risk
money borrowed to finance the farm business
natural resources available for farming
physical labour performed on the farm
questions.explanation: The management/entrepreneurial factor coordinates land, labour, and capital into productive use, makes key decisions, and bears the risk of the farming enterprise.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: The reward earned by land as a factor of production is called
options: wages
rent
interest
profit
questions.explanation: Rent is the payment made for the use of land, distinguishing it from wages (labour), interest (capital), and profit (management/entrepreneurship).

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: The reward earned by labour as a factor of production is called
options: profit
rent
wages
interest
questions.explanation: Wages are the payment made to labour for its physical or mental effort applied in the production process.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: The reward earned by capital as a factor of production is called
options: profit
wages
rent
interest
questions.explanation: Interest is the return earned on capital invested in a productive enterprise, distinct from rent (land) and wages (labour).

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: The reward earned by management/entrepreneurship as a factor of production is called
options: interest
wages
profit
rent
questions.explanation: Profit is the reward that accrues to the entrepreneur/manager for organising production and bearing business risk.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Farm records are kept mainly to help the farmer
options: guarantee immunity from crop or livestock loss
monitor farm performance, costs, and profitability over time
avoid paying any form of taxation permanently
eliminate the need for hired farm labour
questions.explanation: Accurate farm records allow a farmer to track inputs, outputs, income, and expenses, supporting sound decisions and future planning.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: An inventory record on a farm mainly lists the
options: farm's assets, such as livestock, equipment, and stock of produce, with their values
daily weather conditions on the farm
market prices of competing farms' produce
names of neighbouring farmers
questions.explanation: An inventory record catalogues everything the farm owns, land, buildings, machinery, livestock, and stored produce, together with their estimated value.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: A labour record on a farm is mainly used to track
options: the number of workers, hours worked, and wages paid for various farm operations
the chemical composition of the soil
the market price of farm produce
the varieties of crops planted
questions.explanation: Labour records document who worked, for how long, on which tasks, and what wages were paid, helping the farmer assess labour costs and efficiency.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: A cash book, as used in farm accounting, is mainly used to record
options: the number of livestock born during the year
the physical quantity of crops harvested only
the types of pests found on the farm
all cash receipts and payments made by the farm business
questions.explanation: The cash book chronologically records every cash inflow (sales, receipts) and outflow (purchases, expenses) of the farm business.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: A farm balance sheet mainly shows the
options: daily rainfall recorded on the farm
farm's total sales for a particular season only
list of workers employed on the farm
farm's assets, liabilities, and net worth at a specific point in time
questions.explanation: A balance sheet is a financial statement summarising what the farm owns (assets), what it owes (liabilities), and the resulting net worth (equity) at a given date.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: A profit and loss (income) statement in farm accounting mainly shows the
options: number of animals treated for disease
types of crops grown in rotation
farm's total income and expenses over a given period, and the resulting profit or loss
farm's total land area under cultivation
questions.explanation: The profit and loss statement summarises revenue earned and expenses incurred over a specific period, revealing whether the farm made a profit or a loss.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Complete budgeting in farm management involves
options: estimating the weather for the coming season
planning the entire farm's operations and finances for a future period
adjusting only one small part of an existing farm plan
recording only past farm transactions
questions.explanation: A complete budget covers the whole farm business, projecting all expected income, expenses, and resource use for the upcoming production period.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Partial budgeting in farm management is used mainly to
options: calculate the farm's total land size
evaluate the financial effect of a specific, limited change to an existing farm plan
record the farm's historical rainfall data
plan the entire farm's operations from scratch
questions.explanation: Partial budgeting analyses only the costs and benefits of a proposed change (e.g., switching part of a field to a new crop) rather than the whole farm plan.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Depreciation, as recorded in farm accounts, refers to the
options: increase in the market value of livestock over time
gradual reduction in the value of a farm asset (e.g., machinery) over its useful life
sudden total loss of an asset due to theft
cost of feeding farm animals
questions.explanation: Depreciation accounts for the gradual decline in value of durable assets like tractors and buildings as they wear out or become obsolete over time.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Which of the following best describes the purpose of farm accounting?
options: Systematically recording and analysing the financial transactions of the farm business
Breeding and selecting improved livestock
Physically planting and harvesting crops
Controlling pests and diseases on the farm
questions.explanation: Farm accounting focuses specifically on tracking and analysing money, income, expenditure, assets and liabilities, distinct from the physical operations of farming.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Agricultural marketing covers all activities involved in the
options: actual cultivation and harvesting of crops
breeding of improved crop and livestock varieties
movement of farm produce from the point of production to the final consumer
application of fertiliser and pesticides to crops
questions.explanation: Agricultural marketing encompasses assembling, grading, transporting, storing, and selling produce until it finally reaches the consumer.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: In the agricultural marketing channel, a wholesaler mainly functions to
options: buy produce in bulk from producers and resell it in smaller quantities to retailers
process raw produce into finished consumer goods only
provide extension advice to farmers
grow crops directly for sale to consumers
questions.explanation: Wholesalers act as intermediaries, purchasing large quantities of produce from producers and breaking it down for sale to retailers or other buyers.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: In the agricultural marketing channel, a retailer mainly functions to
options: produce raw agricultural commodities on a farm
buy produce only in very large bulk quantities for export
sell farm produce directly to the final consumer in small quantities
set national agricultural policy
questions.explanation: Retailers are the final link in the marketing chain, selling produce in small, consumer-sized quantities directly to the end buyer.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Marketing cooperatives assist farmers mainly by
options: eliminating the need for farmers to grow any crops
setting the weather conditions for the season
pooling produce together to gain better bargaining power and access to markets
replacing agricultural extension officers
questions.explanation: By combining the output of many small farmers, cooperatives can negotiate better prices, access larger markets, and reduce individual marketing costs.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Marketing boards, historically established in West Africa for crops like cocoa and groundnut, mainly functioned to
options: grow crops directly on behalf of the government
control the weather to improve crop yields
provide free farm machinery to all farmers
regulate the purchase, pricing, and export of specified agricultural commodities
questions.explanation: Marketing boards were government-established bodies that controlled the buying, pricing, and export of key cash crops, aiming to stabilise farmer incomes and generate revenue.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Grading, as a marketing function, refers to the
options: storage of produce to prevent spoilage
transportation of produce from farm to market
financing of farm inputs
sorting of produce into different classes based on quality or size
questions.explanation: Grading sorts produce into standard quality or size classes, helping to set appropriate prices and meet buyer preferences.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Processing, as a marketing function, adds value to raw agricultural produce mainly by
options: storing it in its raw form indefinitely
reducing its price to attract more buyers
simply transporting it to the nearest market
converting it into a more usable or durable form, such as turning cassava into garri
questions.explanation: Processing transforms raw produce into a more convenient, durable, or marketable form, adding value and often extending shelf life.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Packaging, as a marketing function, is important mainly because it
options: eliminates the need for storage facilities
increases the natural ripening rate of fruit
replaces the need for transportation
protects produce from damage and makes it more attractive and convenient for buyers
questions.explanation: Proper packaging shields produce from physical damage and contamination during handling and transport, while also improving its market appeal.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Transportation, as a marketing function, mainly serves to
options: move produce from areas of production to areas of demand
reduce the actual quantity of produce harvested
eliminate the need for grading and packaging
improve the taste and quality of produce directly
questions.explanation: Transportation bridges the geographic gap between where produce is grown and where it is needed by consumers or processors, and is a key marketing cost.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Storage, as a marketing function, mainly helps to
options: eliminate the need for any form of transportation
immediately increase the size of harvested produce
replace the need for financing of farm produce
hold produce until it is needed, reducing glut and spoilage at harvest time
questions.explanation: Storage allows produce to be kept safely after harvest and released to the market gradually, smoothing out supply and helping avoid post-harvest glut and waste.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Financing, as a marketing function in agriculture, mainly involves
options: grading produce according to size
regulating rainfall patterns for farmers
growing crops directly for the market
providing funds needed to move produce through the marketing chain, from production to sale
questions.explanation: Financing supplies the capital needed by marketing intermediaries and farmers to purchase, store, transport, and process produce before it is finally sold.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Agricultural extension is best described as the
options: collection of taxes from farmers by government
process of growing crops for direct sale to consumers
process of transferring useful agricultural knowledge and skills from research institutions to farmers
manufacture of farm machinery and equipment
questions.explanation: Extension serves as the vital link between agricultural research and practising farmers, disseminating improved technologies and practices to raise productivity.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: The individual method of agricultural extension teaching involves
options: a direct, one-on-one contact between the extension agent and a single farmer
addressing a large audience through radio broadcasts
organising a large field demonstration for many farmers
distributing printed materials to an entire community at once
questions.explanation: The individual (or farm-and-home visit) method involves personalised, one-on-one interaction between the extension agent and a single farmer, allowing tailored advice.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: The group method of agricultural extension teaching involves
options: communicating with only a single farmer at a time
broadcasting information through television to an unspecified audience
publishing findings only in scientific journals
reaching a number of farmers together, such as through meetings, demonstrations, or field days
questions.explanation: The group method brings together a cluster of farmers for meetings, method demonstrations, or field days, allowing shared learning and discussion.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: The mass media method of agricultural extension teaching involves reaching farmers mainly through
options: one-on-one farm visits only
individual farm records only
small discussion groups of five farmers
radio, television, newspapers, and similar channels
questions.explanation: Mass media methods use radio, television, print, and similar channels to disseminate agricultural information quickly to a large, widespread audience of farmers.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: One of the major roles of an agricultural extension officer is to
options: manufacture agricultural equipment for sale
educate farmers on new and improved farming techniques and technologies
set the market price of all agricultural produce
collect government taxes from rural farmers
questions.explanation: Extension officers primarily educate and advise farmers, translating agricultural research findings into practical guidance farmers can adopt.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: A major barrier to effective agricultural extension work in West Africa is
options: excessive funding provided to extension programmes
the complete absence of any farmers willing to learn
poor rural infrastructure, such as roads, that limits access to remote farming communities
the total absence of agricultural research institutions
questions.explanation: Poor roads and limited infrastructure in many rural areas make it difficult for extension agents to regularly reach and support farmers in remote communities.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Illiteracy among farmers is often cited as a barrier to agricultural extension mainly because it
options: eliminates the need for extension services entirely
increases farmers' income automatically
makes farmers immune to all crop diseases
limits farmers' ability to read and understand written extension materials
questions.explanation: Low literacy levels can prevent farmers from benefiting fully from printed extension materials, requiring greater reliance on oral, visual, or demonstration-based methods.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: The adoption of improved farming technologies by farmers in West Africa is sometimes hindered by
options: an overabundance of fertile farmland everywhere
conservative attitudes and reluctance to depart from traditional farming practices
excessive availability of agricultural credit
an oversupply of extension officers in every village
questions.explanation: Deeply rooted traditional beliefs and risk-aversion can make some farmers hesitant to adopt new methods or technologies promoted by extension services.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: A method demonstration, used in agricultural extension teaching, mainly involves
options: distributing seeds without any guidance
broadcasting a general talk on the radio
showing farmers, step by step, how to carry out a specific farming practice
collecting written feedback from farmers by post
questions.explanation: A method demonstration teaches farmers a specific skill (e.g., correct fertiliser application) by showing them exactly how to perform it, step by step.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: A result demonstration, used in agricultural extension work, is mainly intended to
options: teach farmers how to keep farm records
train farmers in first aid techniques
regulate the price of farm produce in the market
show farmers the actual benefits/results of adopting a new practice compared to their old one
questions.explanation: Result demonstrations compare an improved practice against the farmer's usual method on an actual plot, convincing farmers by showing tangible results side by side.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Limited access to agricultural credit is a common problem affecting the adoption of extension recommendations mainly because farmers
options: already possess unlimited financial resources
may lack the funds needed to purchase improved inputs like seeds and fertiliser
have no interest in improving their farming methods
do not require any inputs to adopt new practices
questions.explanation: Even when farmers are willing to adopt improved practices, a lack of affordable credit can prevent them from purchasing the necessary inputs, such as improved seed and fertiliser.
